1000362.etyen:
Borrowed from Italian Firenze (“Florence”), from Old Italian Fiorenze (“Florence”), ultimately from Latin Flōrentiae (“at Florence”), the locative of Flōrentia (“Florence”). The change from pretonic fio- to fi- reflects a characteristic Florentine reduction. Forms of the modern type are attested in medieval Tuscany from the mid-thirteenth century, including Firençe (1255), Firenzzie (1287) and Firense (1304). The archaic and literary Italian form Fiorenza (“Florence”) preserves the older initial diphthong.
The Latin place name Flōrentia (“Florence”) was formed from flōrēns (“blooming, flourish

1000618.etyen:
From Bosnia (“Bosnia”) + Hercegovina (“Herzegovina”), with the hyphen joining two coordinate elements and functioning like og (“and”), literally “Bosnia and Herzegovina”.
The first element, Bosnia, is an international form ultimately based on Serbo-Croatian Bȍsna, the name of the river after which the historical region was named. The deeper origin of the river name is uncertain. The pronunciation with [ɔ] instead of expected [ʊ] is rather learned.

1004714.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Ǫlvér m, also found as Ǫlvir m, from Proto-Norse *Aluwīhaz m. The first element has been interpreted as meaning “luck; protection” and the second as “giant, warrior”. Alternatively, the name has been connected with words meaning “sanctuary” and “priest”, giving an original meaning such as “chief priest”.
Compare Alver, which may represent another Norwegian development of the same name, as well as Icelandic Ölvir and Swedish Ölver.

en.g: a surname originating as a patronymic, originally meaning “son of Håvard”
x: Senere lærte han en rekke slåtter av blant andre Knut Dahle, Vilhelm Sorteberg, Kjetil Håvardson, valdrisene Olav Moe og Jørn Røn.
Later he learned a number of fiddle tunes from, among others, Knut Dahle, Vilhelm Sorteberg, Kjetil Håvardson, the Valdres musicians Olav Moe and Jørn Røn.

1004970.etyen:
From Håvard (“male given name”) + -son (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Håvard”.
The given name Håvard goes back to Old Norse Hávarðr, for which two Proto-Norse preforms have been reconstructed: *Hauhawarduz, literally “high guardian”, and *Haþuwarduz, literally “battle guardian”. The second element of both forms continues Proto-Germanic *warduz (“guard, guardian”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to heed, watch”).
Compare Icelandic Hávarðarson and Faroese Hávarðarson (“patronymics”).
